title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

reading.body:
State Farm's defense lawyers submitted legal filings containing fabricated case citations, fake quotes, and nonexistent legal holdings in a lawsuit brought by a homeowner over delays in fire damage repairs. The lawyers used an AI tool called Irys to prepare the filings and mistakenly believed it performed accuracy checks when it did not. Seven case citations across eight filings were later found not to exist.

This is a failure of verification at the deployment stage. The lawyers relied on an AI system to generate legal research without human review of the factual claims it made. What would have caught this was checking each cited case against an actual legal database before filing, a standard practice in legal work that was bypassed. The system was used in conditions where accuracy was essential and hallucination unacceptable, yet no guardrail existed between its output and court submission.

It is not established whether the AI tool was designed or marketed as performing the accuracy checks the lawyers believed it did.

reports.title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
AI hallucinated case law in insurance company’s filings in L.A. County house fire dispute
AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

summary:
State Farm's defense lawyers apologized after admitting they used artificial intelligence to prepare legal filings that contained fabricated case citations, fake quotes, and nonexistent legal holdings in a lawsuit filed by Los Angeles homeowner Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga. The homeowner sued State Farm and other defendants after a 2020 fire in her Carson home caused extensive damage, and subsequent delays in getting repair approvals led to incomplete restoration work. She and her husband subsequently lost their savings, retirement accounts, and home to foreclosure.

Lawyer Jacquelene Robinson acknowledged that seven case citations across eight filings did not actually exist, and she mistakenly believed an AI tool called Irys performed accuracy checks when it did not. The firm's lead counsel accepted responsibility for the filings and said the firm updated its AI policies. The case is scheduled for trial in October. This incident reflects a growing problem in the legal field, where 41 percent of law firms now use generative AI, with a database documenting 1,922 legal hallucination cases worldwide, mostly in the United States.
